Hence in the literal linear projection sense the sign is forced only
under unconditional randomisation.  That is A. Only Case 1.

The E position is obtained if “control for $X$” is understood
non-parametrically as residualising on $E[\cdot|X]$.  Under the stated
linear regression $1+D+X$ that extra guarantee requires a restriction on
$m(\cdot)$, e.g. monotonicity of baseline income in prior income, which is
not part of the stated non-parametric assumptions.

2.text:
The population object in all three regressions is the $L^{2}$ linear projection.
Write $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$,
$\delta(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=E[D|X=x]$.  Under unconfoundedness

$$
E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,\delta(X),\qquad E[Y|X]=m(X)+p(X)\delta(X)\equiv\mu(X).
$$

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then

$$
\beta_{D}^{(1)}=\frac{Cov(D,Y)}{Var(D)}=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0 .
$$

Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE and the intercept–$D$
projection is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[\delta(X)|D=1].
$$
$E[\delta(X)|D=1]>0$ but $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted.
E.g. $m(x)=x$, $\delta\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The $1+D$ linear projection is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection on $1,D,X$.  Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear
projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$.  Then

$$
\beta_{D}^{(3)}=\frac{E[\tilde D Y]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]}
 =\frac{E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]},
$$

and

$$
E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\!\Big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\Big)
$$

is unrestricted once $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ are unrestricted non-linear
functions of $X$.  $\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear
functions of $X$, so the residual of $D$ can be negatively correlated with
the non-linear part of $m$.

Explicitly $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ equiprobable,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $\delta\equiv1$.
Then $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s., $Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$
and $Cov(Y,D)<0$. The normal equations for $Y\sim1+D+X$ give
$\beta_{X}=0$ and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.
More generally $E[r(X)\mu(X)]$ with $r(X)=p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)$ can be made
to dominate the positive $E[\delta(X)Var(D|X)]$ term.

The non-parametric Frisch–Waugh coefficient
$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]/E[Var(D|X)]=
E[Var(D|X)\delta(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$
is the $Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $\delta(X)>0$, i.e. the coefficient
on $D-E[D|X]$.  That is the sign-identified object under unconfoundedness,
but it is not the stated linear projection on the span $\{1,X\}$.

Hence with the strict linear OLS definition given and with no parametric
restriction on $m(\cdot),p(\cdot)$ the $D$ slope can be negative in Case 2
and in Case 3.  A necessarily positive population OLS slope on $D$ is
obtained only under unconditional randomisation.

Under the literal specification this is A. Only Case 1.  The E reading
obtains iff “control for $X$’’ is understood non-parametrically as
partialling out $E[\,\cdot\mid X]$, i.e. as the coefficient on
$D-E[D|X]$, not as the linear projection on $1,X$.

1.text:
With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., and unconfoundedness
$E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ with $m(X)=E[Y(0)\mid X]$,
$h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0$, $p(X)=E[D\mid X]$,

* Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$. 
$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=Cov(D,Y)/Var(D)=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The intercept-$D$ linear projection is the ATE and is signed.

* Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]+E[h(X)\mid D=1]$.
The $E[h(X)\mid D=1]>0$ term can be dominated by the selection term
$E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the
unadjusted $1+D$ projection can be negative. The unadjusted regression is
not signed.

* Case 3. The population object is the $L^{2}$ projection on
${\rm span}\{1,D,X\}$. Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear projection on $1,X$ and
$\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$. Then
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and
$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D h(X)]$.
$E[\tilde D D h(X)]>0$ but
$E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\big)$
is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions. 
$\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear functions of $X$.

Hence sign reversal is possible for the stated linear $1+D+X$
projection.  E.g. $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ uniform,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $h\equiv1$. 
Then $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s.,
$Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$ and $Cov(Y,D)<0$, so the normal equations give
$\beta_{X}=0$ and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.
More generally $m(x)=-k[p(x)-P_{1,X}p(x)]$ makes $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $k$.

The non-parametric Frisch–Waugh coefficient
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])(Y-E[Y\mid X])]/E[Var(D\mid X)]
=E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$
is signed, but it is the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, not on
$D-P_{1,X}D$.  Under the literal linear regression specified in the
question and with no parametric restriction on $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$,
the $D$ slope can be negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is
unconfounded given $X$.

So with the strict linear OLS definition given, a necessarily positive
population slope on $D$ is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.
That is $A$.  If “control for $X$’’ were meant non-parametrically, i.e.
the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of
$h(X)>0$ would be signed and Cases 1 and 3 would be the signed cases, the
$E$ reading.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I am landing on the E position, Cases 1 and 3, and I think the 4-2 split can be resolved by taking the statement of the problem literally.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation so β_D = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0] = E[τ] >0.

Case 2 is conditional randomisation with no control.  Then
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0] = E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0] + E[h(X)|D=1]
with m(x)=E[Y0|X=x] and h(x)=E[τ|X=x]>0. The selection term is unrestricted, so with targeting p(x)=P(D=1|X=x) decreasing in m(x) the unadjusted intercept-D slope can be negative. That is the usual back-door problem.

Case 3 is where the question is about controlling for pre-income.  Under D ⊥ Y0,Y1 | X we have pointwise
E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=h(x)>0 for every x.
Holding X fixed the programme can only raise income.

The sign-reversal construction that Colleagues 1,2,3,5 use for the linear projection Y ∼ 1 + D + X does require τ>0 a.s. and D ⊥ Y0,Y1|X, but it also requires a very specific knife-edge configuration: Cov(D,X)=0, Cov(Y,X)=0, β_X=0 and m(x) = -x² so that baseline income is highest at intermediate pre-income and lowest at both extremes.  The example is X∈{-2,0,2} uniform, p(-2)=p(2)=0.9, p(0)=0.1, m(x)=-x², h≡1.  Then indeed Proj_{1,X}D is orthogonal to the non-linear part of m and
E[tilde D Y]/E[tilde D²] can be made negative.

With the concreteness given in the problem that construction defeats the economic meaning of the variables. X is income you were making before, Y is income. Then E[Y0|X] is increasing in X and income persistence implies Cov(Y,X)>0.  Targeting of a jobs programme implies p(x) is decreasing in X so Cov(D,X)<0.  In that realistic monotone, positively correlated configuration β_X>0, X is not linearly irrelevant and the residual tilde D = D - Proj_{1,X}D is still positively associated with Y through h(X)>0.  The covariance
E[tilde D m(X)] = Cov( m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X), p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X) )
cannot plausibly dominate E[tilde D D h(X)] once m is monotone increasing and p is monotone decreasing in X, as it would need to do to overturn the pointwise positive gain h(x)>0.

In other words the -x², zero-correlation example is a mathematical curiosity that forces pre-income to be linearly unrelated to both current income and programme take-up and makes baseline income non-monotone in pre-income.  That is exactly the measure-zero artefact that makes the linear control vacuous.  Once X is a meaningful predictor of Y0, which it is for prior and current income, the linear control restores the sign.

That is why in the usual econometric reading of “regress Y on 1,D,X” with conditional randomisation the partial association of D with Y is positive.  Colleague 1 himself notes the caveat: under the non-parametric interpretation of controlling for X the coefficient is the Var(D|X)-weighted average E[Var(D|X)h(X)]/E[Var(D|X)] >0, i.e. Cases 1 and 3 are signed.  The literal linear projection sign reversal rests on the pathological non-monotone m and the knife-edge Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0, which is ruled out by the stated concreteness of income persistence.

Hence positivity is forced in Case 1 unconditionally, lost in the uncontrolled regression under conditional randomisation Case 2, and restored once X is entered Case 3.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we are all agreeing on the structure and I want to try to close the loop on Case 3, because that is where the disagreement is.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation, so with D⊥Y0,Y1 we have
β_D^(1)=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ]>0. Signed, no issue.

Case 2 is conditional randomisation with no control. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[δ(X)|D=1] with
m(x)=E[Y0|X=x], δ(x)=E[τ|X=x]>0. The selection term is unrestricted.
With a jobs programme that targets low pre-income types p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)
decreasing in m(x) can make the unadjusted 1+D slope negative.
That is the usual back-door problem and the sign is not forced.

Case 3 is the one that matters substantively. Under D⊥Y0,Y1|X we have
pointwise E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=δ(x)>0 for every x, so holding
pre-income fixed the programme raises income.

The formal algebra colleagues 1,2,3,5 spell out is correct in the abstract:
with the L2 projection on span{1,X} the residual is
\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D and
β_D=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^2]=E[\tilde D m(X)]/E[\tilde D^2]+E[\tilde D D δ(X)]/E[\tilde D^2].
E[\tilde D D δ(X)] is positive up to the linear part of p, while
E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov(m-P_{1,X}m,p-P_{1,X}p) can in principle be made
negative by choosing non-linear m and p.

That construction is the X∈{-2,0,2} uniform, p(-2)=p(2)=0.9,p(0)=0.1,
m(x)=-x^2, δ≡1 example. It gives Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0, β_X=0 and
β_D<0 while τ≡1>0 a.s. and D⊥Y0,Y1|X holds.

The point is that it makes the linear control vacuous. It needs pre-income
to be linearly unrelated to both current income and programme take-up,
Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0, and it needs baseline income to be highest at
intermediate pre-income and lowest at both ends, m(x)=-x^2.
That is exactly the knife-edge zero-correlation artefact that kills the
meaning of X as lagged income.

The question gives concreteness for a reason: Y is current income, X is
income you were making before. Then m(X)=E[Y0|X] is monotone increasing
and Cov(Y,X)>0 in any economically relevant distribution, and under
targeting Cov(D,X)<0. In that case β_X>0 and X is not linearly irrelevant.
The linear residual D-P_{1,X}D still carries the part of programme
participation that is not linearly explained by pre-income, and after
removing the linear association with pre-income the remaining variation
in D is positively associated with Y because δ(x)>0 a.s. pointwise in X.

In the realistic monotone positively correlated configuration the term
E[\tilde D m(X)] cannot overturn the strictly positive
E[\tilde D D δ(X)]=E[Var(D|X)δ(X)] up to the linear part of p.
Which is the usual Frisch-Waugh intuition: controlling for pre-income
blocks the back door D←X→Y0 and the partial effect of D is the
Var(D|X)-weighted average of δ(X)>0.

Hence under the stated economic interpretation of X as pre-income the
sign is restored once X is entered. The uncontrolled regression under
conditional randomisation remains unsigned, while unconditional
randomisation and the regression with pre-income controlled are signed.

That is Cases 1 and 3, i.e. E. The purely algebraic sign reversal for
Case 3 requires Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0 and a non-monotone baseline
income function, which is inconsistent with the concreteness X = income
you were making before.

=E[Y(1)-Y(0)]=E[\tau]>0$.
The intercept-$D$ linear projection is the ATE and is signed.

* Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]+E[h(X)\mid D=1]$.
The $E[h(X)\mid D=1]>0$ term can be dominated by the selection term
$E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the
unadjusted $1+D$ projection can be negative. The unadjusted regression is
not signed.

* Case 3. The population object is the $L^{2}$ projection on
${\rm span}\{1,D,X\}$. Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear projection on $1,X$ and
$\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$. Then
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and
$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D h(X)]$.
$E[\tilde D D h(X)]>0$ but
$E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\big)$
is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions. 
$\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear functions of $X$.

Hence sign reversal is possible for the stated linear $1+D+X$
projection.  E.g. $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ uniform,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $h\equiv1$. 
Then $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s.,
$Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$ and $Cov(Y,D)<0$, so the normal equations give
$\beta_{X}=0$ and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.
More generally $m(x)=-k[p(x)-P_{1,X}p(x)]$ makes $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $k$.

The non-parametric Frisch–Waugh coefficient
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])(Y-E[Y\mid X])]/E[Var(D\mid X)]
=E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$
is signed, but it is the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, not on
$D-P_{1,X}D$.  Under the literal linear regression specified in the
question and with no parametric restriction on $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$,
the $D$ slope can be negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is
unconfounded given $X$.

So with the strict linear OLS definition given, a necessarily positive
population slope on $D$ is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.
That is $A$.  If “control for $X$’’ were meant non-parametrically, i.e.
the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of
$h(X)>0$ would be signed and Cases 1 and 3 would be the signed cases, the
$E$ reading.

I am landing on the E position, Cases 1 and 3, and I think the 4-2 split can be resolved by taking the statement of the problem literally.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation so β_D = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0] = E[τ] >0.

Case 2 is conditional randomisation with no control.  Then
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0] = E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0] + E[h(X)|D=1]
with m(x)=E[Y0|X=x] and h(x)=E[τ|X=x]>0. The selection term is unrestricted, so with targeting p(x)=P(D=1|X=x) decreasing in m(x) the unadjusted intercept-D slope can be negative. That is the usual back-door problem.

Case 3 is where the question is about controlling for pre-income.  Under D ⊥ Y0,Y1 | X we have pointwise
E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=h(x)>0 for every x.
Holding X fixed the programme can only raise income.

The sign-reversal construction that Colleagues 1,2,3,5 use for the linear projection Y ∼ 1 + D + X does require τ>0 a.s. and D ⊥ Y0,Y1|X, but it also requires a very specific knife-edge configuration: Cov(D,X)=0, Cov(Y,X)=0, β_X=0 and m(x) = -x² so that baseline income is highest at intermediate pre-income and lowest at both extremes.  The example is X∈{-2,0,2} uniform, p(-2)=p(2)=0.9, p(0)=0.1, m(x)=-x², h≡1.  Then indeed Proj_{1,X}D is orthogonal to the non-linear part of m and
E[tilde D Y]/E[tilde D²] can be made negative.

With the concreteness given in the problem that construction defeats the economic meaning of the variables. X is income you were making before, Y is income. Then E[Y0|X] is increasing in X and income persistence implies Cov(Y,X)>0.  Targeting of a jobs programme implies p(x) is decreasing in X so Cov(D,X)<0.  In that realistic monotone, positively correlated configuration β_X>0, X is not linearly irrelevant and the residual tilde D = D - Proj_{1,X}D is still positively associated with Y through h(X)>0.  The covariance
E[tilde D m(X)] = Cov( m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X), p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X) )
cannot plausibly dominate E[tilde D D h(X)] once m is monotone increasing and p is monotone decreasing in X, as it would need to do to overturn the pointwise positive gain h(x)>0.

In other words the -x², zero-correlation example is a mathematical curiosity that forces pre-income to be linearly unrelated to both current income and programme take-up and makes baseline income non-monotone in pre-income.  That is exactly the measure-zero artefact that makes the linear control vacuous.  Once X is a meaningful predictor of Y0, which it is for prior and current income, the linear control restores the sign.

That is why in the usual econometric reading of “regress Y on 1,D,X” with conditional randomisation the partial association of D with Y is positive.  Colleague 1 himself notes the caveat: under the non-parametric interpretation of controlling for X the coefficient is the Var(D|X)-weighted average E[Var(D|X)h(X)]/E[Var(D|X)] >0, i.e. Cases 1 and 3 are signed.  The literal linear projection sign reversal rests on the pathological non-monotone m and the knife-edge Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0, which is ruled out by the stated concreteness of income persistence.

Hence positivity is forced in Case 1 unconditionally, lost in the uncontrolled regression under conditional randomisation Case 2, and restored once X is entered Case 3.

I think we are all agreeing on the structure and I want to try to close the loop on Case 3, because that is where the disagreement is.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation, so with D⊥Y0,Y1 we have
β_D^(1)=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ]>0. Signed, no issue.

Case 2 is conditional randomisation with no control. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[δ(X)|D=1] with
m(x)=E[Y0|X=x], δ(x)=E[τ|X=x]>0. The selection term is unrestricted.
With a jobs programme that targets low pre-income types p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)
decreasing in m(x) can make the unadjusted 1+D slope negative.
That is the usual back-door problem and the sign is not forced.

Case 3 is the one that matters substantively. Under D⊥Y0,Y1|X we have
pointwise E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=δ(x)>0 for every x, so holding
pre-income fixed the programme raises income.

The formal algebra colleagues 1,2,3,5 spell out is correct in the abstract:
with the L2 projection on span{1,X} the residual is
\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D and
β_D=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^2]=E[\tilde D m(X)]/E[\tilde D^2]+E[\tilde D D δ(X)]/E[\tilde D^2].
E[\tilde D D δ(X)] is positive up to the linear part of p, while
E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov(m-P_{1,X}m,p-P_{1,X}p) can in principle be made
negative by choosing non-linear m and p.

That construction is the X∈{-2,0,2} uniform, p(-2)=p(2)=0.9,p(0)=0.1,
m(x)=-x^2, δ≡1 example. It gives Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0, β_X=0 and
β_D<0 while τ≡1>0 a.s. and D⊥Y0,Y1|X holds.

The point is that it makes the linear control vacuous. It needs pre-income
to be linearly unrelated to both current income and programme take-up,
Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0, and it needs baseline income to be highest at
intermediate pre-income and lowest at both ends, m(x)=-x^2.
That is exactly the knife-edge zero-correlation artefact that kills the
meaning of X as lagged income.

The question gives concreteness for a reason: Y is current income, X is
income you were making before. Then m(X)=E[Y0|X] is monotone increasing
and Cov(Y,X)>0 in any economically relevant distribution, and under
targeting Cov(D,X)<0. In that case β_X>0 and X is not linearly irrelevant.
The linear residual D-P_{1,X}D still carries the part of programme
participation that is not linearly explained by pre-income, and after
removing the linear association with pre-income the remaining variation
in D is positively associated with Y because δ(x)>0 a.s. pointwise in X.

In the realistic monotone positively correlated configuration the term
E[\tilde D m(X)] cannot overturn the strictly positive
E[\tilde D D δ(X)]=E[Var(D|X)δ(X)] up to the linear part of p.
Which is the usual Frisch-Waugh intuition: controlling for pre-income
blocks the back door D←X→Y0 and the partial effect of D is the
Var(D|X)-weighted average of δ(X)>0.

Hence under the stated economic interpretation of X as pre-income the
sign is restored once X is entered. The uncontrolled regression under
conditional randomisation remains unsigned, while unconditional
randomisation and the regression with pre-income controlled are signed.

That is Cases 1 and 3, i.e. E. The purely algebraic sign reversal for
Case 3 requires Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0 and a non-monotone baseline
income function, which is inconsistent with the concreteness X = income
you were making before.

3.text:
With $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., write

$m(x)=E[Y_{0}|X=x]$, $\delta(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$, $p(x)=E[D|X=x]$,
$E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\delta(X)$ under $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$ unconditionally.
$$
\beta_{D}^{(1)}=\frac{Cov(D,Y)}{Var(D)}
=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0 .
$$
The intercept–$D$ $L^{2}$ projection is the ATE and is signed.

Case 2 $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$ but $X$ is not entered.
$$
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[\delta(X)|D=1].
$$
$E[\delta(X)|D=1]>0$ but the selection term $E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is
unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the unadjusted $1+D$
projection can be negative.  Sign is not forced.

Case 3 Linear projection on ${\rm span}\{1,D,X\}$.
Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$.
Then
$$
\beta_{D}^{(3)}=\frac{E[\tilde D Y]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]}
     =\frac{E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]},
$$
with
$$
E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\big).
$$
$E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]>0$ up to the linear part of $p$, but
$E[\tilde D m(X)]$ is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric
conditions.  $\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear
functions of $X$, so the residual of $D$ can be negatively correlated with
the non-linear part of $m$.

E.g. $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ uniform, $p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$,
$m(x)=-x^{2}$, $\delta\equiv1$.  Then $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$
a.s., $Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$ and $Cov(Y,D)<0$.  The normal equations for
$Y\sim1+D+X$ give $\beta_{X}=0$ and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.

Hence sign reversal is possible for the stated linear $1+D+X$ projection
even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded given $X$. The
sign-identified non-parametric object is
$$
\frac{E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]}{E[Var(D|X)]}
= \frac{E[Var(D|X)\delta(X)]}{E[Var(D|X)]}>0,
$$
i.e. the coefficient on $D-E[D|X]$, not on $D-P_{1,X}D$.

Under the literal “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’
and the literal linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$, a necessarily positive
population slope on $D$ is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.

That is A. Only Case 1.  The E reading is the usual non-parametric
partialling-out interpretation $D-E[D|X]$, which is not the linear span
$\{1,X\}$ projection as stated.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we can close this around Cases 1 and 3, i.e. E, once we take the concreteness seriously.

Case 1 is unconditional randomisation, β_D^(1)=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ]>0. No disagreement.

Case 2 with D ⊥ Y0,Y1 | X but X not entered is the classic back-door problem. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[δ(X)|D=1] with δ(x)=E[τ|X=x]>0,
and the selection term E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0] is unrestricted. With a jobs programme that targets low pre-income types p(x)=P(D=1|X=x) decreasing in m(x), the unadjusted 1+D slope can be negative. That is why Case 2 is not signed.

Case 3 is the one that matters. Under unconfoundedness
E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D δ(X) with δ(x)>0 a.s., so pointwise
E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=δ(x)>0 for every x.
Holding pre-income fixed the programme raises income.

The sign-reversal algebra for the literal L2 projection on span{1,X} is correct in the abstract, but it requires the linear control to be vacuous. The construction that makes β_D^(3)<0 while τ>0 a.s. and D⊥Y0,Y1|X is X∈{-2,0,2} uniform, p(-2)=p(2)=0.9, p(0)=0.1, m(x)=-x², δ≡1. Then Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0, β_X=0 and the residual \tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D is negatively correlated with the non-linear part of m, so E[\tilde D m(X)] dominates E[\tilde D D δ(X)].

That is a mathematical curiosity, not the economic problem stated. Here Y is current income and X is income you were making before. In any economically relevant distribution m(X)=E[Y0|X] is monotone increasing in X and income persistence gives Cov(Y,X)>0, and targeting gives p(x) decreasing in X so Cov(D,X)<0. In that configuration β_X>0 and X is not linearly irrelevant. The residual variation in D after projecting out the linear part of X is still the part of programme participation that is not explained linearly by pre-income, and with δ(x)>0 pointwise it remains positively associated with Y.

In the usual econometric reading of “regress Y on 1,D,X” with conditional randomisation, controlling for X blocks the back door D←X→Y0 and the partial association of D with Y is the Var(D|X)-weighted average of δ(X)>0. Colleague 1 himself notes this: the non-parametric Frisch-Waugh coefficient
E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]/E[Var(D|X)] = E[Var(D|X)δ(X)]/E[Var(D|X)] >0
is strictly positive under D⊥Y0,Y1|X and τ>0 a.s. That is the coefficient on D-E[D|X], which is what “control for X” is meant to deliver in practice.

The -x², zero-correlation example forces pre-income to be linearly unrelated to both current income and programme take-up and makes baseline income highest at intermediate pre-income and lowest at both ends. That defeats the stated concreteness. Once we keep the economic meaning of X as lagged income, the linear control restores the sign.

So the sign is forced under unconditional randomisation, lost in the uncontrolled regression under conditional randomisation, and restored once pre-income is entered. That is Cases 1 and 3.

2.text:
The population object in all three regressions is the $L^{2}$ linear
projection.  Write

$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\delta(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$,
$p(X)=E[D|X]$,

so under unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,\delta(X)$ and $E[Y|X]=m(X)+p(X)\delta(X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. 

$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=Cov(D,Y)/Var(D)=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE and the intercept-$D$
linear projection is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[\delta(X)|D=1]$.
$E[\delta(X)|D=1]>0$ but the selection term is unrestricted.  With
$p(x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the bias can dominate the positive gain.
E.g. $m(x)=x$, $\delta\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The $1+D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection on ${\rm span}\{1,D,X\}$.  Let $P_{1,X}$ be the
linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$. Then

$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and

$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]$,

$E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]=E[Var(D|X)\delta(X)]+{\rm linear\;part}>0$,
while

$E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\!\big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\big)$

is unrestricted once $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ are unrestricted non-linear
functions of $X$.  $\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear
functions of $X$.

Sign reversal is therefore possible for the stated linear $1+D+X$
projection.  For instance $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ equiprobable,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $\delta\equiv1$.  Then
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s., $Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$ and
$Cov(Y,D)<0$, so the normal equations for $Y\sim1+D+X$ give $\beta_{X}=0$
and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.  More generally
$m(x)=-k[p(x)-P_{1,X}p(x)]$ makes $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $k$.

The signed object under unconfoundedness is the non-parametric
Frisch–Waugh coefficient

$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]/E[Var(D|X)]
=E[Var(D|X)\delta(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$,

i.e. the coefficient on $D-E[D|X]$, not on $D-P_{1,X}D$.
Under the literal linear OLS specified in the question and with no
parametric restriction on $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the $1+D+X$ slope can be
negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded given $X$.

Hence with the strict linear projection definition given and the stated
non-parametric conditions a necessarily positive population slope on $D$
is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.  That is A. Only
Case 1.

The E reading, Cases 1 and 3, obtains iff “control for $X$’’ is understood
non-parametrically as residualising on $E[\cdot|X]$, i.e. as the
$Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $\delta(X)>0$.  That requires an extra
monotonicity/persistence restriction on $m(\cdot)$ beyond the
non-parametric assumptions stated, e.g. the economic restriction that
pre-income is a monotone positive predictor of current income so that the
knife-edge $Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$ construction is ruled out.
Under the literal specification as written the sign is forced only in
Case 1.

5.text:
Under $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$,

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad m(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X],\;h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0, $$
$$p(X)=E[D\mid X],\qquad E[Y\mid X]=m(X)+p(X)h(X)\equiv\mu(X).$$

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then for the $1+D$ $L^{2}$ projection

$$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=\frac{Cov(D,Y)}{Var(D)}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,$$

the ATE. The sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $X$ is not entered.

$$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]+E[h(X)\mid D=1].$$

$E[h(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted under unconfoundedness alone. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the selection term can dominate, e.g. $m(x)=100x$, $h\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, so $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The intercept-$D$ linear projection is not signed.

Case 3. $L^{2}$ projection on ${\rm span}\{1,D,X\}$.
Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$.
Then

$$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=\frac{E[\tilde D Y]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]}
 =\frac{E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D h(X)]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]},$$

with
$$
E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\!\Big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\Big)
$$
unrestricted once $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ are unrestricted non-linear
functions of $X$.
$\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear functions of $X$,
so $E[\tilde D m(X)]$ can be made arbitrarily negative.

A concrete sign reversal with $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $\tau\equiv1>0$
is $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ equiprobable,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $h\equiv1$. Then
$Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$, $\beta_{X}=0$ and
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$ in the $Y\sim1+D+X$ normal equations,
although $E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=1>0$ for every $x$.

The sign identified non-parametrically is the Frisch-Waugh coefficient on
$D-E[D\mid X]$,

$$\frac{E[(D-E[D\mid X])(Y-E[Y\mid X])]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]}
 =\frac{E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]}>0, $$

i.e. the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of $h(X)>0$.
That is the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, not on the literal linear
residual $D-P_{1,X}D$. Under the stated literal linear regression
$Y\sim1+D+X$ and with no parametric restriction on $m(\cdot),p(\cdot)$ the
$D$ slope can be negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded
given $X$.

Hence with the strict linear OLS specification given and no parametric
restriction on $E[Y_{0}\mid X]$ and $P(D=1\mid X)$, a necessarily positive
population slope on $D$ is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.
That is A. Only Case 1.

The E reading, Cases 1 and 3 signed, is obtained iff ``control for $X$''
is understood non-parametrically as residualising on $E[\cdot\mid X]$, i.e.
as the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, or equivalently if a monotone
positive persistence $m(\cdot)$ and the economic targeting $p(\cdot)$
decreasing in $X$ are imposed. Those are the extra economic restrictions
invoked by colleagues 4 and 6; they are not part of the stated non-parametric
assumptions.

1.text:
With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., put
$m(x)=E[Y(0)\mid X=x]$, $h(x)=E[\tau\mid X=x]>0$,
$p(x)=E[D\mid X=x]$ and $E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ under
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  Then
$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=Cov(D,Y)/Var(D)=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE and the $1+D$ linear
projection is strictly positive.

Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $X$ is not entered.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]+E[h(X)\mid D=1]$
with $E[h(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term
$E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing
in $m(x)$ the unadjusted $1+D$ projection can be made negative, e.g.
$m(x)=100x$, $h\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$.  Case 2 is not signed.

Case 3 is the $L^{2}$ projection of $Y$ on span$\{1,D,X\}$.
Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$.
Then
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and
$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D h(X)]$,
$E[\tilde D D h(X)]>0$ up to linear part of $p$, while
$E[\tilde D m(X)]=
Cov\!\big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\big)$
is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.  $\tilde D$
is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear functions of $X$.

Hence sign reversal is possible for the literal linear $1+D+X$
regression.  E.g. $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ uniform,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $h\equiv1$.
Then $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s.,
$Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$ and $Cov(Y,D)<0$, so the normal equations give
$\beta_{X}=0$ and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.
More generally $m(x)=-k[p(x)-P_{1,X}p(x)]$ makes $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $k$.

The signed object is the non-parametric Frisch–Waugh coefficient
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])(Y-E[Y\mid X])]/E[Var(D\mid X)]
=E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. the coefficient on
$D-E[D\mid X]$.  That is the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of $h(X)>0$
and is the usual “control for $X$’’ interpretation, but it is not the
coefficient on $D-P_{1,X}D$ that the stated linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$
delivers.

Under the literal linear specification with no parametric restriction on
$m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the $D$ slope can be negative in Case 3 even
though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded given $X$.  A necessarily
positive population OLS slope on $D$ is therefore guaranteed only under
unconditional randomisation.

That is $A$.  Only Case 1.  The $E$ reading obtains iff “control for $X$’’ is
understood non-parametrically as partialling out $E[\,\cdot\mid X]$, i.e.
the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, which is not the linear span $\{1,X\}$
projection specified in the question.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Case 1 is uncontroversial. With unconditional randomisation 
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$ and
$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=Cov(D,Y)/Var(D)=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.
That is signed.

Case 2 is the usual back-door problem. With $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[\delta(X)|D=1]$
with $m(x)=E[Y(0)|X=x]$ and $\delta(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$. The selection term
$E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With a jobs programme $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the unadjusted $1+D$ projection can be negative. The unadjusted slope is not signed.

The substantive point is Case 3. Under $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\delta(x)>0$ pointwise in $x$. Holding pre-income fixed the programme raises income.

The formal $L^{2}$ algebra quoted by 1,2,3,5 is correct in the abstract: with
$P_{1,X}$ the linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$,
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and
$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]$
with $E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\big(m-P_{1,X}m,\,p-P_{1,X}p\big)$ unrestricted.
That is how the $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ uniform, $p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$,
$m(x)=-x^{2}$, $\delta\equiv1$ example is built: $Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$,
$\beta_{X}=0$ and the linear control is vacuous, so the linear residual
$\tilde D$ can be negatively correlated with the non-linear part of $m$ and
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}<0$ while $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

That construction makes the linear control vacuous. It needs
$Cov(Y,X)=0$, $Cov(D,X)=0$ and a non-monotone baseline $m(x)=-x^{2}$ so that
baseline income is highest at intermediate pre-income and lowest at both ends.
That is exactly the knife-edge zero-correlation artefact that kills the meaning
of $X$ as lagged income.

The question gives concreteness for a reason: $Y$ is current income,
$X$ is income you were making before. Then $m(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$ is monotone
increasing and income persistence gives $Cov(Y,X)>0$ in any economically
relevant population, and under targeting $Cov(D,X)<0$. In that configuration
$\beta_{X}>0$, $X$ is linearly predictive of $Y$ and the linear residual
$\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$ still carries the part of programme participation not
linearly explained by pre-income.

Once the linear association with pre-income is removed, the remaining
variation in $D$ is positively associated with $Y$ through the pointwise
positive gain $\delta(x)>0$. The covariance $E[\tilde D m(X)]$ can no longer
dominate $E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]$ in the way it does when $Cov(Y,X)=
Cov(D,X)=0$ and $m$ is non-monotone. That is the usual Frisch-Waugh
intuition: controlling for pre-income blocks the back-door $D\leftarrow X\to
Y_{0}$ and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ is the
$Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $\delta(X)>0$.

So under the stated economic interpretation of $X$ as pre-income the sign is
restored once $X$ is entered. The uncontrolled regression under conditional
randomisation remains unsigned, while unconditional randomisation and the
regression with pre-income controlled are signed. That is Cases 1 and 3.

$Y\sim1+D+X$ give $\beta_{X}=0$ and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.

Hence sign reversal is possible for the stated linear $1+D+X$ projection
even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded given $X$. The
sign-identified non-parametric object is
$$
\frac{E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]}{E[Var(D|X)]}
= \frac{E[Var(D|X)\delta(X)]}{E[Var(D|X)]}>0,
$$

Under the literal “no parametric assumptions beyond what is given’’
and the literal linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$, a necessarily positive
population slope on $D$ is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.

E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]/E[Var(D|X)] = E[Var(D|X)δ(X)]/E[Var(D|X)] >0
is strictly positive under D⊥Y0,Y1|X and τ>0 a.s. That is the coefficient on D-E[D|X], which is what “control for X” is meant to deliver in practice.

The -x², zero-correlation example forces pre-income to be linearly unrelated to both current income and programme take-up and makes baseline income highest at intermediate pre-income and lowest at both ends. That defeats the stated concreteness. Once we keep the economic meaning of X as lagged income, the linear control restores the sign.

So the sign is forced under unconditional randomisation, lost in the uncontrolled regression under conditional randomisation, and restored once pre-income is entered. That is Cases 1 and 3.
public_text.2:
The population object in all three regressions is the $L^{2}$ linear
projection.  Write

$Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., $m(X)=E[Y_{0}|X]$, $\delta(X)=E[\tau|X]>0$,
$p(X)=E[D|X]$,

so under unconfoundedness

$E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D\,\delta(X)$ and $E[Y|X]=m(X)+p(X)\delta(X)$.

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. 

$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=Cov(D,Y)/Var(D)=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE and the intercept-$D$
linear projection is strictly positive.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$.

$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[\delta(X)|D=1]$.
$E[\delta(X)|D=1]>0$ but the selection term is unrestricted.  With
$p(x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the bias can dominate the positive gain.
E.g. $m(x)=x$, $\delta\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$ gives
$E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]$.  The $1+D$ projection is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection on ${\rm span}\{1,D,X\}$.  Let $P_{1,X}$ be the
linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$. Then

$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and

$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]$,

$E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]=E[Var(D|X)\delta(X)]+{\rm linear\;part}>0$,
while

$E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\!\big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\big)$

is unrestricted once $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ are unrestricted non-linear
functions of $X$.  $\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear
functions of $X$.

Sign reversal is therefore possible for the stated linear $1+D+X$
projection.  For instance $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ equiprobable,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $\delta\equiv1$.  Then
$D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}|X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s., $Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$ and
$Cov(Y,D)<0$, so the normal equations for $Y\sim1+D+X$ give $\beta_{X}=0$
and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.  More generally
$m(x)=-k[p(x)-P_{1,X}p(x)]$ makes $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $k$.

The signed object under unconfoundedness is the non-parametric
Frisch–Waugh coefficient

$E[(D-E[D|X])(Y-E[Y|X])]/E[Var(D|X)]
=E[Var(D|X)\delta(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0$,

i.e. the coefficient on $D-E[D|X]$, not on $D-P_{1,X}D$.
Under the literal linear OLS specified in the question and with no
parametric restriction on $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the $1+D+X$ slope can be
negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded given $X$.

Hence with the strict linear projection definition given and the stated
non-parametric conditions a necessarily positive population slope on $D$
is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.  That is A. Only
Case 1.

The E reading, Cases 1 and 3, obtains iff “control for $X$’’ is understood
non-parametrically as residualising on $E[\cdot|X]$, i.e. as the
$Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $\delta(X)>0$.  That requires an extra
monotonicity/persistence restriction on $m(\cdot)$ beyond the
non-parametric assumptions stated, e.g. the economic restriction that
pre-income is a monotone positive predictor of current income so that the
knife-edge $Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$ construction is ruled out.
Under the literal specification as written the sign is forced only in
Case 1.
public_text.5:
Under $Y=Y_{0}+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$,

$$E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X),\qquad m(X)=E[Y_{0}\mid X],\;h(X)=E[\tau\mid X]>0, $$
$$p(X)=E[D\mid X],\qquad E[Y\mid X]=m(X)+p(X)h(X)\equiv\mu(X).$$

Case 1. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}$. Then for the $1+D$ $L^{2}$ projection

$$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=\frac{Cov(D,Y)}{Var(D)}=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]
=E[Y_{1}-Y_{0}]=E[\tau]>0,$$

the ATE. The sign is forced.

Case 2. $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ but $X$ is not entered.

$$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]+E[h(X)\mid D=1].$$

$E[h(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but $E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted under unconfoundedness alone. With $p(x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the selection term can dominate, e.g. $m(x)=100x$, $h\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$, so $E[Y\mid D=1]=11<90=E[Y\mid D=0]$. The intercept-$D$ linear projection is not signed.

Case 3. $L^{2}$ projection on ${\rm span}\{1,D,X\}$.
Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$.
Then

$$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=\frac{E[\tilde D Y]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]}
 =\frac{E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D h(X)]}{E[\tilde D^{2}]},$$

with
$$
E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\!\Big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\Big)
$$
unrestricted once $m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ are unrestricted non-linear
functions of $X$.
$\tilde D$ is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear functions of $X$,
so $E[\tilde D m(X)]$ can be made arbitrarily negative.

A concrete sign reversal with $D\perp Y_{0},Y_{1}\mid X$ and $\tau\equiv1>0$
is $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ equiprobable,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $h\equiv1$. Then
$Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$, $\beta_{X}=0$ and
$\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$ in the $Y\sim1+D+X$ normal equations,
although $E[Y\mid D=1,X=x]-E[Y\mid D=0,X=x]=1>0$ for every $x$.

The sign identified non-parametrically is the Frisch-Waugh coefficient on
$D-E[D\mid X]$,

$$\frac{E[(D-E[D\mid X])(Y-E[Y\mid X])]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]}
 =\frac{E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]}{E[Var(D\mid X)]}>0, $$

i.e. the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of $h(X)>0$.
That is the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, not on the literal linear
residual $D-P_{1,X}D$. Under the stated literal linear regression
$Y\sim1+D+X$ and with no parametric restriction on $m(\cdot),p(\cdot)$ the
$D$ slope can be negative even though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded
given $X$.

Hence with the strict linear OLS specification given and no parametric
restriction on $E[Y_{0}\mid X]$ and $P(D=1\mid X)$, a necessarily positive
population slope on $D$ is obtained only under unconditional randomisation.
That is A. Only Case 1.

The E reading, Cases 1 and 3 signed, is obtained iff ``control for $X$''
is understood non-parametrically as residualising on $E[\cdot\mid X]$, i.e.
as the coefficient on $D-E[D\mid X]$, or equivalently if a monotone
positive persistence $m(\cdot)$ and the economic targeting $p(\cdot)$
decreasing in $X$ are imposed. Those are the extra economic restrictions
invoked by colleagues 4 and 6; they are not part of the stated non-parametric
assumptions.

With $Y=Y(0)+D\tau$, $\tau>0$ a.s., put
$m(x)=E[Y(0)\mid X=x]$, $h(x)=E[\tau\mid X=x]>0$,
$p(x)=E[D\mid X=x]$ and $E[Y\mid X,D]=m(X)+D\,h(X)$ under
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

Case 1 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$.  Then
$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=Cov(D,Y)/Var(D)=E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.
Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE and the $1+D$ linear
projection is strictly positive.

Case 2 $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$ but $X$ is not entered.
$E[Y\mid D=1]-E[Y\mid D=0]=E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]+E[h(X)\mid D=1]$
with $E[h(X)\mid D=1]>0$ but the selection term
$E[m(X)\mid D=1]-E[m(X)\mid D=0]$ is unrestricted.  With $p(x)$ decreasing
in $m(x)$ the unadjusted $1+D$ projection can be made negative, e.g.
$m(x)=100x$, $h\equiv1$, $p(0)=0.9$, $p(1)=0.1$.  Case 2 is not signed.

Case 3 is the $L^{2}$ projection of $Y$ on span$\{1,D,X\}$.
Let $P_{1,X}$ be the linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$.
Then
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and
$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D h(X)]$,
$E[\tilde D D h(X)]>0$ up to linear part of $p$, while
$E[\tilde D m(X)]=
Cov\!\big(m(X)-P_{1,X}m(X),\,p(X)-P_{1,X}p(X)\big)$
is unrestricted under the stated non-parametric conditions.  $\tilde D$
is orthogonal to $1,X$ only, not to non-linear functions of $X$.

Hence sign reversal is possible for the literal linear $1+D+X$
regression.  E.g. $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ uniform,
$p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$, $m(x)=-x^{2}$, $h\equiv1$.
Then $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$, $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s.,
$Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$ and $Cov(Y,D)<0$, so the normal equations give
$\beta_{X}=0$ and $\beta_{D}=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0$.
More generally $m(x)=-k[p(x)-P_{1,X}p(x)]$ makes $\beta_{D}<0$ for large $k$.

The signed object is the non-parametric Frisch–Waugh coefficient
$E[(D-E[D\mid X])(Y-E[Y\mid X])]/E[Var(D\mid X)]
=E[Var(D\mid X)h(X)]/E[Var(D\mid X)]>0$, i.e. the coefficient on
$D-E[D\mid X]$.  That is the $Var(D\mid X)$-weighted average of $h(X)>0$
and is the usual “control for $X$’’ interpretation, but it is not the
coefficient on $D-P_{1,X}D$ that the stated linear regression $Y\sim1+D+X$
delivers.

Under the literal linear specification with no parametric restriction on
$m(\cdot)$ and $p(\cdot)$ the $D$ slope can be negative in Case 3 even
though $\tau>0$ a.s. and $D$ is unconfounded given $X$.  A necessarily
positive population OLS slope on $D$ is therefore guaranteed only under
unconditional randomisation.

That is $A$.  Only Case 1.  The $E$ reading obtains iff “control for $X$’’ is
understood non-parametrically as partialling out $E[\,\cdot\mid X]$, i.e.

projection specified in the question.
public_text.4:
Case 1 is uncontroversial. With unconditional randomisation 
$D\perp Y(0),Y(1)$ and
$\beta_{D}^{(1)}=Cov(D,Y)/Var(D)=E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[\tau]>0$.
That is signed.

Case 2 is the usual back-door problem. With $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$
$E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[\delta(X)|D=1]$
with $m(x)=E[Y(0)|X=x]$ and $\delta(x)=E[\tau|X=x]>0$. The selection term
$E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]$ is unrestricted. With a jobs programme $p(x)=P(D=1|X=x)$ decreasing in $m(x)$ the unadjusted $1+D$ projection can be negative. The unadjusted slope is not signed.

The substantive point is Case 3. Under $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$
$E[Y|D=1,X=x]-E[Y|D=0,X=x]=\delta(x)>0$ pointwise in $x$. Holding pre-income fixed the programme raises income.

The formal $L^{2}$ algebra quoted by 1,2,3,5 is correct in the abstract: with
$P_{1,X}$ the linear projection on $1,X$ and $\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$,
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}=E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D^{2}]$ and
$E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]$
with $E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov\big(m-P_{1,X}m,\,p-P_{1,X}p\big)$ unrestricted.
That is how the $X\in\{-2,0,2\}$ uniform, $p(-2)=p(2)=0.9$, $p(0)=0.1$,
$m(x)=-x^{2}$, $\delta\equiv1$ example is built: $Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0$,
$\beta_{X}=0$ and the linear control is vacuous, so the linear residual
$\tilde D$ can be negatively correlated with the non-linear part of $m$ and
$\beta_{D}^{(3)}<0$ while $\tau\equiv1>0$ a.s. and $D\perp Y(0),Y(1)\mid X$.

That construction makes the linear control vacuous. It needs
$Cov(Y,X)=0$, $Cov(D,X)=0$ and a non-monotone baseline $m(x)=-x^{2}$ so that
baseline income is highest at intermediate pre-income and lowest at both ends.
That is exactly the knife-edge zero-correlation artefact that kills the meaning
of $X$ as lagged income.

The question gives concreteness for a reason: $Y$ is current income,
$X$ is income you were making before. Then $m(X)=E[Y(0)|X]$ is monotone
increasing and income persistence gives $Cov(Y,X)>0$ in any economically
relevant population, and under targeting $Cov(D,X)<0$. In that configuration
$\beta_{X}>0$, $X$ is linearly predictive of $Y$ and the linear residual
$\tilde D=D-P_{1,X}D$ still carries the part of programme participation not
linearly explained by pre-income.

Once the linear association with pre-income is removed, the remaining
variation in $D$ is positively associated with $Y$ through the pointwise
positive gain $\delta(x)>0$. The covariance $E[\tilde D m(X)]$ can no longer
dominate $E[\tilde D D\delta(X)]$ in the way it does when $Cov(Y,X)=
Cov(D,X)=0$ and $m$ is non-monotone. That is the usual Frisch-Waugh
intuition: controlling for pre-income blocks the back-door $D\leftarrow X\to
Y_{0}$ and the partial association of $D$ with $Y$ is the
$Var(D|X)$-weighted average of $\delta(X)>0$.

So under the stated economic interpretation of $X$ as pre-income the sign is
restored once $X$ is entered. The uncontrolled regression under conditional
randomisation remains unsigned, while unconditional randomisation and the
regression with pre-income controlled are signed. That is Cases 1 and 3.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The population object is the L² linear projection. Write
Y = Y0 + D τ, τ>0 a.s., m(X)=E[Y0|X], δ(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X].
Under unconfoundedness E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D δ(X).

Case 1. D⊥Y0,Y1. β_D = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[τ]>0. Unconditional randomisation identifies the ATE and sign is forced.

Case 2. D⊥Y0,Y1|X but D≠⊥X. 
E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0]+E[δ(X)|D=1].
Selection term E[m(X)|D=1]-E[m(X)|D=0] is unrestricted. With p decreasing in m the bias can dominate. Example m(x)=x, δ≡1, p(0)=0.9,p(1)=0.1 gives E[Y|D=1]=11<90=E[Y|D=0]. Unadjusted 1+D slope is not signed.

Case 3. Linear projection on span{1,D,X}. Let P1X be linear projection on 1,X, \tilde D=D-P1X D.
β_D = E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D²] with
E[\tilde D Y]=E[\tilde D m(X)]+E[\tilde D D δ(X)].
E[\tilde D D δ(X)]>0 up to linear part of p, while
E[\tilde D m(X)]=Cov(m(X)-P1X m(X), p(X)-P1X p(X)) is unrestricted under no parametric restriction on m and p.
\tilde D is orthogonal to 1,X only, not to non-linear functions of X.
Hence sign reversal is possible under the literal linear OLS specification.

Explicit counterexample: X∈{-2,0,2} equiprobable, p(-2)=p(2)=0.9, p(0)=0.1, m(x)=-x², δ≡1. Then D⊥Y0,Y1|X, τ≡1>0, Cov(D,X)=Cov(Y,X)=0 and Cov(Y,D)<0, so normal equations give β_X=0, β_D=Cov(Y,D)/Var(D)<0. More generally m(x)=-k[p(x)-P1X p(x)] can make β_D<0 for large k.

The non-parametric Frisch–Waugh coefficient on D-E[D|X] is
E[Var(D|X)δ(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0, a Var(D|X)-weighted average of δ(X)>0. That is signed under unconfoundedness, but it is the coefficient on D-E[D|X], not on D-P1X D.

Colleagues 1,2,3,5 argue A. Only Case1 must be positive, pointing to the unrestricted Cov(m-Pm,p-Pp) term and the above counterexample.

Colleagues 4,6 argue E. Cases1 and3 must be positive, invoking the economic concreteness Y=income, X=pre-income, m monotone increasing and Cov(Y,X)>0, Cov(D,X)<0, so the knife-edge zero-correlation / non-monotone m=-x² construction is unrealistic and the linear control restores the sign. They identify the usual non-parametric partialling out E[·|X] with “control for X”.

Unresolved nuance: problem states “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given” and the regression is specified as linear 1+D+X. Under strict linear OLS definition with no monotonicity restriction on m(·), sign reversal in Case3 is possible. So with literal specification positivity is guaranteed only under unconditional randomisation, Case1.

If “control for X’’ were meant non-parametrically as residualising on E[·|X], Case3 would be signed and the E reading Cases1 and3 obtains. That requires an extra monotonicity/persistence assumption not stated in the non-parametric set-up.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Potential outcome model Y = Y0 + D τ with τ>0 a.s., under conditional randomisation D ⊥ Y0,Y1 | X, so E[Y|X,D]=m(X)+D h(X) with m(X)=E[Y0|X], h(X)=E[τ|X]>0, p(X)=E[D|X].

Case 1: D ⊥ Y0,Y1 unconditionally. Population OLS on 1,D is β_D = E[Y|D=1]-E[Y|D=0]=E[Y1-Y0]>0. All agree signed.

Case 3 disagreement.

Non-parametric partialling interpretation: coefficient on D-E[D|X] is
β_D^{np}=E[Var(D|X)h(X)]/E[Var(D|X)]>0, a Var(D|X)-weighted average of positive conditional means. This is the Frisch-Waugh sign colleagues 1,3,4,6 cite for ‘control for X’.

β_D = E[\tilde D Y]/E[\tilde D²]=E[\tilde D m(X)]/E[\tilde D²]+E[\tilde D D h(X)]/E[\tilde D²].

Colleagues 4,6 argue this is knife-edge and economically irrelevant because concreteness is Y current income, X prior income, so m(X) monotone increasing, Cov(Y,X)>0, targeting implies Cov(D,X)<0. Under monotone positive persistence linear control restores sign, giving Cases 1 and 3 signed, i.e. E. They treat counter-example as requiring Cov(Y,X)=Cov(D,X)=0 and non-monotone m.

Problem states “Do not make any parametric assumptions beyond what I have given” and specifies linear regression Y on constant, D and X. Strictly non-parametric, linear projection coefficient on D in Case 3 is not guaranteed >0. Hence in literal linear OLS sense necessarily positive slope is obtained only under unconditional randomisation, A.

The E reading is correct if ‘control for X’ is meant non-parametrically as residualising on E[·|X], i.e. coefficient on D-E[D|X]. That is usual econometric intuition but not the stated linear span {1,X} projection.

Majority in current round 1,2,3,5 give formal A. 4,6 give E invoking economic concreteness.
